the problem of force-sharing among the fingers in the grasping task is well-posed with respect to the inverse problem, and the objective function that is obtained from the experimental data can predict the force sharing for a wide range of external forces.

(1) the force-sharing problem can be solved by the method of inverse optimization, (2) the force-sharing task is optimized by a quadratic objective function with essentially non-zero first-order terms, (3) the force-sharing objective function is different for different types of grasps, and (4) the force-sharing pattern predicted by this objective function is in a good agreement with experimental data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of what are the objective functions that underlie different motor actions in humans.
the problem of what humans are optimizing in their actions.
the problem of finding the objective functions that are responsible for human motor control.

our method is a useful tool to analyze the problem of inverse human motor optimization.
the objective function is not a simple function of the finger force magnitudes, but rather a function of the finger forces and their directions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the problem of inverse human optimization can be solved analytically and that the resulting objective functions can predict human behavior with high accuracy.
the objective functions for human motor actions are not necessarily linear and that the linear models are not necessarily good approximations of the objective functions.
the objective function in a grasping action is a quadratic function with essentially non-zero first-degree terms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the objective function for a motor task is unique up to an additive constant.
it is possible to find an objective function that can explain a wide range of experimental data and, moreover, that this function is not necessarily linear.
it is possible to obtain a unique solution for the inverse optimization problem for human motor actions with additive objective functions.
